DWB labels it a pronoun when it means “personally”. The Duden labels it a particle in both senses.}@^ is generally understood to refer to the subject of the clause,whatever its position. Thus ''ich habe Sandra @^ gefragt'' means “I myself asked Sandra”,and not “I asked Sandra herself”. This can only be changed by placing the object at the beginning of the clause:''Sandra @^ habe ich gefragt'' (“Sandra herself was the one I asked”).

*Selbstentfremdung*German{}|Etymology}selbst+Entfremdung|Pronunciation}/ˈzɛlpstɛntfʁɛmdʊŋ/|Noun}(fem.)}#self-alienation,self-estrangement}#} & w:Friedrich Engels|title The Holy Family|original w:de:Die heilige Familie|chapter IV. KAPITEL|trans-chapter Chapter IV|passage Die besitzende Klasse und die Klasse des Proletariats stellen dieselbe menschliche '''@^''' dar. Aber die erste Klasse fühlt sich in dieser '''@^''' wohl und bestätigt,weiß die Entfremdung als ihre eigne Macht und besitzt in ihr den Schein einer menschlichen Existenz; die zweite fühlt sich in der Entfremdung vernichtet,erblickt in ihr ihre Ohnmacht und die Wirklichkeit einer unmenschlichen Existenz. |translation The propertied class and the class of the proletariat present the same human '''self-estrangement'''. The class of the proletariat feels annihilated in estrangement; it sees in it its own powerlessness and the reality of an inhuman existence.

*Selbstverkleinerung*German{}2014|Etymology}selbst+Verkleinerung|Pronunciation}/ˈzɛlpstfɛɐ̯ˌklaɪ̯nəʁʊŋ/|Noun}(fem.)}#self-dwarfing}•synononym:Selbstverzwergung}•Antonym:Prahlerei}#}'''1886''',Friedrich Wilhelm Nietzsche,''Jenseits von Gut und Böse'',Neuntes Hauptstück. Was ist vornehm,267}#}:Es gibt ein Sprichwort bei den Chinesen,das die Mütter schon ihre Kinder lehren:siao-sin »mache dein Herz klein!« Dies ist der eigentliche Grundhang in späten Zivilisationen:ich zweifle nicht,daß ein antiker Grieche auch an uns Europäern von heute zuerst die '''@^''' herauserkennen würde – damit allein schon gingen wir ihm »wider den Geschmack«.+The Chinese have a proverb which mothers even teach their children:"Siao-sin" ("make thy heart small"). This is the essentially fundamental tendency in latter-day civilisations. I have no doubt that an ancient Greek,also,would first of all remark the '''self-dwarfing''' in us Europeans of to-day--in this respect alone we should immediately be "distasteful" to him.

*sexy*German{}|Etymology}from Proto-Indo-European ⋆sek-}Borrowed en.|Pronunciation}/ˈzɛksi/qualifier:official standard but rarely used; usually considered overly formal or incorrect}/ˈsɛksi/qualifier:usual}Ⓓe/e2/De-@^.ogg|Adjective}#@^|Usage notes}In German,most people try to approximate the original pronunciations of many recently borrowed words,which is why there is even a term for this,Fremdwort,for which there is no real equivalent in English. In the case of the corresponding noun,''Sex'',a voiced beginning is considered even more outdated or incorrect than for the adjective ''@^'',and this voiced pronunciation is used and emphasized for sechs ("six") to clearly differentiate it.}The positive form is not inflected in standard usage:''ein @^ Kleid''. Inflected forms only occur in colloquial speech (''ein @^es Kleid''),and only rarely.}The comparative has to be inflected when used before nouns. This is avoided in standard usage,which means that the comparative is rare except in predicative position. (Colloquial:''Sie will ein @^eres Kleid.''/''Sie will ein Kleid,das mehr @^ ist.'' Formal written:''Die Kundin sucht ein Kleid,das @^er ist.'' Formal spoken since the ending of ''@^er'' is hard to hear:''Die Kundin sucht ein Kleid,das mehr @^ ist.'')|Derived terms}un@^

*sich*German{}|Etymology}From Middle High German @^,from Old High German sih,from Proto-Germanic ⋆sek. Compare from Yiddish זיך,from Dutch zich.}This pronoun was originally restricted to the accusative case,while simple personal pronouns were used in the dative. Dative use of from Middle High German @^ in from Middle High German - was restricted to northern dialects of Central German. In Early Modern German,a rare dative sir also occurred,formed by analogy with mir,dir. An obstacle to the generalisation of this form was the use of  in the plural,where there operated the conflicting analogy with the merged accusative/dative forms uns,euch.|Pronunciation}/zɪç/}Ⓓe/ea/De-@^.ogg}Ⓓ0/08/De-@^2.ogg}Rhymes:ɪç|Pronoun}#reflexive pronoun Reflexive pronoun of the third person singular:herself,himself,themself,itself,oneself (''direct'' or ''indirect object'')}#reflexive pronoun Reflexive pronoun of the third person plural:themselves (''direct'' or ''indirect object'')

*Sie*German{}|Alternative forms}-se|Pronunciation}/ziː/}Ⓓ7/72/De-&_.ogg}sie}Rhymes:iː|Pronoun}#you polite; singular and plural}•Was möchten '''&_''',Frau Wagner?}•What would '''you''' like to have,Mrs. Wagner?|Usage notes}The German ''&_'' expresses distance in the relation between two persons. It is not perfectly correct to say that it expresses respect.  has never been used to address gods and saints. Towards parents it was only briefly used during the 18th century by some of the upper classes. (In both of these cases,however,Ihr was formerly possible alongside du.) Even royal highnesses used to be addressed as ''du'',albeit not personally but in songs and poems (compare the famous "w:Heil dir im &_gerkranz").}''&_'' is identical in form to the third person plural pronoun sie and takes the same verb form. The "polite" ''&_'' is distinguished in writing by capitalization. The only form which is not capitalized is the reflexive sich. When addressing a person with ''&_'',one generally needs to replace the third person plural pronoun with the demonstrative die ("those ones") to avoid confusion:''Wissen &_,was '''die''' zu mir gesagt haben?'' − “Do you know what they said to me?”|Derived terms}siezen|Anagrams}Eis||Pennsylvania German{}|Etymology}Compare from German &_.|Pronunciation}/siː/|Pronoun}#you qualifier:polite

*sien*German{}|Pronunciation}/ziːn/|Pronoun}#Form of [sier]||Low German{}|Alternative forms}seyn,syn}sön Low Prussian|Etymology}From Middle Low German sîn,from Old Saxon sīn. The infinitive  along with the words is and sünd derive ultimately from Proto-Indo-European to be,which had no separate infinitive in Germanic. The modern infinitive was probably back-formed in late Old Saxon from the former first-person plural subjunctive from Old Saxon we be,since this form had become identical to the infinitive in other verbs during the late Old Saxon period. Compare also from German sein,from Dutch zijn.}The original infinitive is wesen,from Middle Low German wesen,from Old Saxon wesan,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆wesan,from Proto-Germanic ⋆wesaną,from Proto-Indo-European to reside. All the forms with initial ''w-'' (imperative and past tense) derive from this root. The infinitive wesen is still the most used one,but in general which one is used is a matter of personal preference and/or region.}Finally,the forms bün and büst derive from Proto-Germanic to be,to become,from Proto-Indo-European to become,which survives only as relic forms in the West Germanic languages and not at all in the others. Its infinitive and non-singular forms are only attested in (Old) English.|Pronunciation}/ziːn/|Verb}(''past singular'' '''weer''',''past participle'' '''wesen''' or ''west'',''auxiliary verb'' '''wesen''')}#only as the infinitive alternative form of [wesen]|Synonyms}wesen|See also}wesen
*Siepen*German{}|Alternative forms}Siefen|Etymology}From Middle Low German sîpe,from the verb from Middle Low German tto trickle. Cognate with from Middle High German sīfe,whence the alternative forms,and further with from Dutch tcanal,sewer.|Pronunciation}/ˈziːpən/|Noun}m:n)}#regional a swampy gorge,a brook in a valley|Usage notes}In official toponyms the regional distribution of the forms is roughly as follows:}in Low German and Low Franconian areas,chiefly the w:Bergisches Land and w:Sauerland.}in the Central German parts of North Rhine-Westphalia (except w:Siegerland).}in other Central German areas.}Appellative use outside of purely local contexts is rare in Standard German,but it appears that the proper form  is actually the least favoured,without doubt because of its homonymy with . German wikipedia uses w:langde as lemma,which we follow here.

*Sinn machen*German{}|Etymology}Recorded in earlier rare use by Goethe,Lessing,Luther,and others,including "''Petrus der maister Lampardus,der die '''sentencias @r-5t''',das ist das puch von hochen synnen zu teutsch''." From Medieval Latin (scholasticism) "from Latin sententiam facere".}has seen increasingly widespread use since the 1970s,probably due to the influence of the English expression make sense. Thus,the German expression is probably an interesting example of a rare case of a combination of a resurrected phrase and a modern loan translation. It is now widely used and is listed in Duden as belonging to the colloquial language register.|Pronunciation}/zɪn ˈmaxn̩/+/zɪn ˈmaxən/|Verb}#intransitive to make sense}•synononym:[@-6haben],[@-6ergeben],[sinnvoll sein]

*Sitz im Leben*German{}|Etymology}Coined by Hermann Gunkel in 1930. Literally:[seat in life].|Noun}Sitz<m> im Leben,strong)}#idiomatic sociological setting|Usage notes}Though sometimes rendered by phrases like "life setting","situation in life" etc. the German term ''@^'' is better translated by "sociological setting" or left untranslated. As a technical term,it refers to the social setting of a text,particularly in the Bible. It is primarily used today in academic contexts,especially theology and biblical studies.

*Spekulatius*German{}|Etymology}unk:de. Various theories have been proposed:}Latinized form of Low German (especially East Frisian) ''Spikelātsje'',''Spekelātsje'' and Rhinelandic ''Spekulaties'' (19th c.),from  cog:speculatie meaning "plastically formed goodies" and later referred to "figured biscuits". One possible explanation for the Latinization of the Low German and Rhinelandic forms is that they were believed to be derived from m+:mirror,image,so that Latinization of these forms could take place.}From m+:spy,scout,which gave rise to the word ''Speculator'',which was the byname of Saint Nicholas. The reference to spying,scouting is comparable to Saint Nicholas' act of looking into the windows of poor families to help them out.|Pronunciation}/ʃpekuˈlaːt͡si̯ʊs/}Ⓓf/f4/De-@^.ogg|Noun}(mask.,genitive:@^,plural:[@^])}#speculoos

The sense “haste” is intelligible because of the related verb ,whereas the sense “success” requires special knowledge of Low German.

*sputen*German{}|Etymology}17th century,at first alongside spuden,both secondary adaptations of from Middle Low German spôden,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆spōdijan,derived from Proto-West Germanic prosperity,success,itself from the verb from Proto-West Germanic ⋆spōan,from Proto-Germanic to prosper,succeed,be happy,from Proto-Indo-European to prosper,turn out well. The West Germanic verb had a cognate in from Old High German spuoten,which however remained without continuation. *ß*German{}|Alternative forms}rare|Pronunciation}s:phoneme/s/}s:letter name/ɛsˈtsɛt/Eszett,usual}s:letter name/ˈʃarfəs ˈɛs/scharfes S,less desirable because it also refers to the sound IPAchar:/s/regardless of its spelling|Letter}#Eszett or scharfes S,a German letter based on a ligature of '''ſ''' (long s) and '''z'''.|Usage notes}In alphabetic ordering,'''&_''' is equivalent to the string '''ss'''. For example,one would order:Maske,Ma&_,Masse,Ma&_e,Massen,Ma&_en,Mast. The letter also alternates with '''ss''' in inflections and derivatives,e.g. lassen → past tense lie&_,though such cases are now fairly rare.}The current rules for the choice between '''&_''' and '''ss''' were introduced in 1996. They follow the simple principle that '''ss''' is used after short vowels and '''&_''' otherwise (i.e. after long vowels and diphthongs). Hence  IPAchar:/ˈmasə/is distinguished from  IPAchar:/ˈmaːsə/. The earlier rules were more complicated and less phonetic. They prescribed that '''&_''' was additionally used in the syllable coda regardless of vowel length. Thus küssen,but ,and Fa&_,but Fässer (modern spelling küsst,Fass). The older spelling has become rare,but is still used by some older language users.}In Switzerland and Liechtenstein,the letter '''&_''' is not used at all. So Stra&_e is spelt Strasse,and the above distinction between  and  is lost in favour of the latter. This use is also often seen in Luxembourg and occasionally in South Tyrol,but '''&_''' is standard in both of these areas. Moreover one encounters the same spelling in German books printed in w:antiqua script until the early 20th century,because an antiqua '''&_''' did not yet exist. A rarer alternative was to replace '''&_''' with '''sz'''.}It is standard to replace '''&_''' with '''SS''' in all caps:. However,in 2017 a new uppercase '''ẞ''' was introduced,so it is now also correct to spell . The use of a lowercase '''&_''' () is sometimes seen,but is proscribed. In capitalizing a few words which would become ambiguous if '''&_''' were changed to '''SS''','''SZ''' may be used instead,hence ''MASZE'' (''Ma&_e'') may be kept distinct from ''MASSE'' (''Masse''),''BUSZE'' (''Bu&_e'') from ''BUSSE'' (''Busse'').|Synonyms}Buckel-S}Doppel-S}Dreierles-S}Eszett}Ringel-S}Rucksack-S}scharfes S}Stra&_en-S

*ss*German{}|Symbol}#Sometimes used to replace the letter ß,especially when this key or character is not available. It was also the only official way of writing a capital '''ß''',until '''ẞ''' was officially adopted by the Council for German Orthography in June 2017.}#fromSLDE|Usage notes}In alphabetic ordering,the letter '''ß''' is equivalent to the string '''&_''' (formerly '''sz'''),so aß is sorted between Aspirin and Ast,immediately after the alphabetically equivalent A&_. The letter is never used in Swi&_ or Liechtenstein German,where it is always replaced by &_. Furthermore,ß was unique among the letters of the Latin alphabet as there was no capital form until ẞ was adopted in June 2017; in all-caps,all instances of ß were officially replaced by '''SS'''. However,not every instance of SS can be substituted back into ß.}Since the orthography reform from 1996,the letter ß is used only after long vowels and diphthongs. Before 1996,ß could also occur after short vowels at the end of a word or before a consonant. A rather large number of words that used to be spelled with ß ia now spelled with &_ (for example,daß has become da&_).|Synonyms}ß}Eszett}sz

*staunen*German{}|Etymology}Attested since the 17th century,then introduced in the general written language by Albrecht von Haller (1708-1777),from gsw,of uncertain origin. Probably related to stauen. Alternatively—though less likely both on semantic and phonetic grounds—from Old French estoner,whence from English astound,from English astonish. Probably not related to from English stun (from German stöhnen).}The original sense is “to become stiff,stand still”,used especially of the eyes and thus “to muse,contemplate,romanticise” (from German sinnen,schwärmen,schwelgen),which is the sense in which Haller used it. Outside of Switzerland,however,the word was reinterpreted by backformation from the derivative er@^,which had already been in general use since the 16th century.|Pronunciation}/ˈʃtaʊ̯nən/}Ⓓ/1/10/De-at-@^.ogg(Austria)(Austria)}Ⓓf/fb/De-@^.ogg}stau+nen|Verb}#to be amazed or astonished; to wonder or marvel}•Die Zuschauer '''staunten''' über seine Kunststücke.}•The spectators '''were amazed''' at his tricks and feats.|Usage notes}and erstaunt sein are stronger than sich wundern,but weaker than verblüfft sein. Moreover,they usually imply a degree of admiration,though this is not necessarily the case.|Derived terms}er@^

*Stegreif*German{}|Alternative forms}misspelling|Etymology}From Middle High German tstirrup,from Old High German tstirrup,from Old High German stegōn (“to ascend”,related with from Old High German stīgan,whence modern steigen)+from Old High German reif (“rope,ring”,whence modern Reif). Cognate with from English stirrup.}The contemporary sense is from the idea of someone going to task “from the stirrup”,that is immediately after their arrival and without further arrangements. Speakers now often reanalyse the word as stehen+greifen,that is “something nearby that one grabs wherever one is standing”. Hence the common pronunciation (see below) and the frequent misspelling Stehgreif.|Pronunciation}/ˈʃteːkˌʁaɪ̯f/,(etymological; prescriptive standard)}/ˈʃteːˌɡʁaɪ̯f/,(more common in practice)}Ⓓ2/2e/De-@^.ogg}Steg+reif|Noun}(mask.,plural:[@^s][s][es])}#often improvisation,impromptu}•synononym:[Improvisation],[Lamäng],[(colloquial) regional]}•aus dem '''@^'''}•Ich hatte meine Aufzeichnungen vergessen und musste mir aus dem '''@^''' etwas überlegen.}•I'd forgotten to take my notes and had to make something up by '''improvisation'''.}•Das Gedicht ist eine '''@^'''-Schöpfung.}•The poem is an '''impromptu''' composition.}#obsolete stirrup}•synononym:Steigbügel|Derived terms}aus dem @^

*stein-*German{}|Etymology}From Stein. Originally used in semantically transparent forms like steinalt,steinhart,steintaub,steintot,etc. Then generalised to other adjectives without a semantic relation to the basic word,such as steinreich. *Storch*German{}|Alternative forms}Stork|Etymology}From Middle High German storch,from Middle High German storc,from Old High German storah,from Old High German ⋆storc(h),from Proto-West Germanic ⋆stork,from Proto-Germanic ⋆sturkaz.}Cognate to dialectal from Dutch stork,from English stork,from Swedish stork. The expected German form is also Stork,which was indeed in wide use,but has not become standardized. The shifted variant  is probably due to the use of epenthetic vowels in Old High German,by which the uninflected stem from Old High German storah alternated with inflected from Old High German storc-. Such variation was generally levelled in favour of the inflected stem,but this was an apparent exception. Compare for the regular development from Old High German starah alongside from Old High German starc(h),whence from Middle High German starc and modern stark. Alternatively,could be an Upper German relict form (with rx from rkx),but the regional distribution does not seem to confirm this.|Pronunciation}/ʃtɔrç/+ʃtɔʁç+ʃtɔɐ̯ç+ʃtɔːç}Ⓓc/c0/De-@^.ogg|Noun}(mask.,genitive:@^es,plural:[@^e],diminituve:@^)}#stork Literally:[bird]|Derived terms}col-auto:Weißstorch

*Straßenbahn*German{}|Etymology}From @-5.|Pronunciation}/ˈʃtraːsənˌbaːn/+ˈʃtʀaːsn̩ˌbaːn+ˈʃtʀaːsənˌbaːn+ˈʃtraːsn̩ˌbaːn+ˈʃtraːsənˌbaːn}^Ⓓ2/24/De-@^.ogg|Noun}(fem.)}#streetcar,tramway}•synononym:[Elektrische (dated)],[;],[Tram (Austria],[ Switzerland)],[;],[Trambahn],[;],[Tramway (Austria)],[;],[Straba (Saxony — Würzburg)]|Usage notes}An urban train might drive on the streets on paths that are also used by cars,or it might move in tracks separated from the rest of the road traffic in an open-air area called Gleiskörper,and it might drive underground in tunnels. It depends on the city whether the very same trains drive on all three tracks or whether there are different trains for the three types of tracks. In the latter case,as in Berlin,one w:distinguishes the three types by name,calling the one driving with the cars ''@^'',the one on exclusive tracks S-Bahn,the ones serving the subway U-Bahn. Whereas in Cologne,(English) there is an indistinct @^,U-Bahn or w:Stadtbahn,the w:S-Bahn being a means of transportation of greater distance to connect the whole urban area with its multiple cities. But in places where there isn’t such a tripartite system and a single train moves between tracks used by cars,exclusive s-train-tracks and tunnels in a single route,it is called @^ indistinctly,or also Stadtbahn,this last especially by the officials themselves,so in Bielefeld,the terms S-Bahn and U-Bahn being uncommon,the city being w:surrounded by rural areas otherwise only having busses for local traffic. Whereas in Hamburg “w:@^” is a historical term since the @^en proper have been abolished completely by 1978.|Descendants}only in Germany itself
